title: Drone Attack Sinks Ship Off Bulgaria, Second Strike in a Week
excerpt: The Ukrainian-owned Chelsea 3 was damaged and its 15 crew rescued after three drone hits near the Bulgarian coast, as Sofia summons Russia's ambassador and seeks talks with NATO.
body:
• Two ships were hit by drones off Bulgaria's Black Sea coast on October 13, and one of them sank, according to Prime Minister Rumen Radev.
  • The Ukrainian-owned, Maltese-flagged Chelsea 3 was struck by three drones about 18 nautical miles offshore; all 15 crew members were rescued and none was seriously injured.
  • Radev said there is no clear evidence of who carried out the attack, but said the outcome benefits Russia, and he plans to summon the Russian ambassador and speak to NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte.
  • It was the second such incident off Bulgaria in a week, following the October 6 attack in which the Alfa Watan sank and the Able caught fire.

Two merchant ships were hit by drones off Bulgaria's Black Sea coast in the early hours of October 13, and one of them sank, Prime Minister Rumen Radev said in a televised address. The attack, reported by Al Jazeera and in a Reuters report carried by Devdiscourse, is the second incident of its kind near Bulgarian waters in a week and has drawn a sharp response from Sofia and Brussels.

What happened to the Chelsea 3

The Ukrainian-owned Chelsea 3, sailing under a Maltese flag, was struck by three drones at about 1:30 a.m. local time, roughly 18 nautical miles — about 33 kilometres — off the Bulgarian coast. The vessel was damaged but did not sink. Its crew of 15, made up of seven Ukrainians and eight Azerbaijanis, was rescued. Five crew members received medical assistance, but Radev said none was seriously injured.

The second vessel hit in the same attack sank. Radev said one crew member from the sunken ship was also rescued. He did not, in the remarks reported so far, give a full account of that vessel's crew, its flag, or its cargo.

"absolutely unacceptable"

— Rumen Radev, Prime Minister of Bulgaria

Bulgaria points, carefully, toward Moscow

Radev stopped short of formally blaming any country. He said there was no clear evidence identifying the perpetrator, but added that the outcome of the attack benefits Russia. On that basis, he said, Bulgaria will summon the Russian ambassador over the incident. He also said he is due to speak with NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte.

European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen condemned the attacks on the merchant ships, saying the Black Sea had become another front in the escalation of Russia's war in Ukraine and that those responsible should be held accountable. She thanked Bulgarian rescuers for their response.

A pattern in the Black Sea

The strike follows a similar incident on October 6, when drones hit two ships off Bulgaria — the Alfa Watan, which sank, and the Able, which caught fire. Two attacks in seven days, both close to the waters of a NATO member state, raise the risk that commercial shipping far from the front lines in Ukraine is becoming a routine target.

Bulgaria does not border either Russia or Ukraine, but as a NATO member it holds a strategic position on the western Black Sea, where both belligerents operate major ports and where grain, fuel, and container traffic moves through contested waters. Attacks that damage or sink civilian vessels near its coast test how the alliance responds to incidents that fall short of a direct strike on a member state.

What happens next

Bulgaria's next steps are diplomatic: the summons of the Russian ambassador and Radev's call with Rutte will show how far Sofia and NATO are prepared to go in attributing the attacks and deterring further ones. Investigators will also need to establish who operated the drones, what the sunken vessel was carrying, and whether its full crew has been accounted for. For shipping companies, the immediate question is practical — whether insurers and captains still treat the western Black Sea as a workable route after two sinkings in a week.
